s: Part five.
Hooks.
This is task statement one point five: apply Agent SDK hooks for tool call interception and data normalization.

By the end of this part, you'll know the main hook events, how a PreToolUse hook answers, how to clean results on the way back, why async hooks can't change anything, and who wins when hooks disagree.
Let's start with a picture.
Think of the counter at a post office.
You bring a parcel.
The clerk weighs it.
Rewrites the address into the format the sorting machines want.
Tells you the customs form is missing.
Or refuses the parcel outright.
You never had to know any of those rules.
And no amount of insisting changes what the clerk does.
Why?
Because the rules live at the counter, not in your head.
Hooks are that counter.
They're placed between the agent and everything it tries to do.
They're code you write that runs at fixed moments.
Before a call goes out.
After a result comes back.
When a worker starts.
When a run ends.
Because they run inside your program, rather than inside the conversation, they take none of the model's attention.
And they can't be argued with.
Two uses follow.
One.
You can stop something happening.
Two.
You can correct the shape of something, on the way out, or on the way back.
A lot of what looks like a model getting a format wrong is really a mismatch nobody put a translator in front of.
The technical version.
Hooks are the one place in an agentic system where you get deterministic control over a nondeterministic actor.
They run in your application process, not in the context window.
So they cost no tokens.
And they can't be talked out of a decision.
The events have real names, and the exam expects you to know the main ones.
Available in both the Python and TypeScript SDKs are these.
PreToolUse.
PostToolUse.
PostToolUseFailure.
UserPromptSubmit.
Stop.
SubagentStart.
SubagentStop.
PreCompact.
PermissionRequest.
And Notification.
TypeScript has a longer list on top, including SessionStart and SessionEnd.
Though those are also reachable from Python, as shell command hooks declared in a settings file.
The notes warn that this list has roughly doubled in a year.
So treat it as a snapshot.
And never assume an unfamiliar event name is invented.
For this domain, six matter most.
One.
PreToolUse, for intercepting a call and rewriting its arguments.
Two.
PostToolUse, for normalising results, and auditing.
Three and four.
SubagentStart and SubagentStop, for tracking and aggregating delegated work.
Five.
Stop, for persisting state at the end of a run.
And six.
PreCompact, for archiving a transcript before it's summarised away.
Stop has two documented jobs.
First, it can save state before exit.
Second, it's also a blocking event.
A Stop hook that rejects prevents Claude from stopping, and continues the conversation.
That second job is the verification gate the configuration chapter builds on.
Now the return shape of a PreToolUse hook.
Every callback receives three things.
The event input.
A tool use id, which links a PreToolUse to the PostToolUse for the same call.
And a context object.
All hook inputs share session_id, cwd, and hook_event_name.
And agent_id and agent_type are filled in when the hook fires inside a subagent.
The return has top-level fields, such as systemMessage and continue. continue is spelled continue_ in Python.
And it has a hookSpecificOutput section.
For PreToolUse, hookSpecificOutput carries a permissionDecision.
That's one of four values: allow, deny, ask, or defer.
Plus a permissionDecisionReason, and an updatedInput.
The pairing rules matter.
One at a time.
Pair updatedInput with allow, to auto-approve the rewritten call.
Pair it with ask, to show the rewrite to the user.
Leave permissionDecision out, and the modified input still applies, under normal permission evaluation.
And defer ignores updatedInput entirely.
You return a new object, rather than changing tool_input in place.
And you return an empty object to allow the call unchanged.
Hooks are registered with a matcher, tested against the tool name.
A hook with no matcher fires for every call of its event type.
Question one.
A scenario from the notes shows why this beats the alternatives.
Here's the scenario.
A compliance agent posts entries to a partner ledger, through a Model Context Protocol server.
The API rejects lowercase currency codes, and any date that is not ISO-8601.
The tool schema documents both rules.
The model gets it right most of the time.
But the failure rate sits near four percent.
Which approach gives a guarantee, rather than an improvement?
Take a second.
The answer.
A PreToolUse hook matched to that tool, that rewrites the arguments and returns updatedInput paired with allow.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a longer tool description with examples.
Why?
It improves the first attempt.
But it stays probabilistic.
Wrong: a PostToolUse hook that explains the rejection.
Why?
It repairs after the damage, with a turn already spent.
Wrong: a system prompt section.
Why?
That's the weakest of all.
The right design uses all three in layers.
Fix the description, so the model usually gets it right.
And normalise in the hook, so the API never sees a bad value.
Deny only input you genuinely can't repair.
And say so in the reason.
Hold on to this line.
PreToolUse sees the call before it happens.
So it can block it, or fix it.
And the model can't argue.
Now the return path.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A support agent's order tool returns raw fields. ordered_at, as an epoch integer, meaning seconds since nineteen seventy. status, as a numeric code. amount_cents.
And tier codes, such as P1.
The agent sometimes quotes the wrong order date, or calls a delivered order processing.
The tool belongs to another team, and can't be changed.
What do you do?
Take a second.
A translator sits between a foreign supplier and a shop assistant.
Instead of teaching the assistant a new language, the translator turns every invoice into plain English before it reaches the counter.
The assistant can't misread words it never sees.
The answer.
In exam terms, PostToolUse runs after the tool returns, and before the model sees the result.
That makes it the normalisation window.
So you write a PostToolUse hook that converts the raw fields into plain values.
A readable date.
A status word, like Delivered.
An amount in dollars.
And even business meaning, such as what a Premium tier entitles the customer to.
The model can't misread what it never sees raw.
No change to the other team's tool.
No extra tool call.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: document every code, and the epoch format, in the system prompt.
Why?
The misreading stays possible.
And the decoding tables compete with everything else in the window.
Wrong: a PreToolUse hook that rewrites the order id.
Why?
That acts on the arguments going in.
But the misreadings come from the result coming back.
Wrong: a separate decode_order tool the agent can call when unsure.
Why?
That adds turns.
And it relies on the model knowing when it's unsure, which is exactly when it doesn't.
Hold on to this line.
Fix confusing results on the way back, in code, before the model reads them.
Next, trimming.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A debugging assistant's log_search tool returns about forty thousand tokens per call.
After four or five searches, the context compacts.
And the assistant loses track of which request ids it was chasing.
It only needs the matching lines, with timestamps and request ids.
But engineers sometimes need the full output afterwards.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
A good assistant opens the post, and hands you only the three letters that matter.
With a note saying the rest is in the tray if you want it.
You never wade through junk mail.
And nothing is thrown away.
The answer.
In exam terms, PostToolUse can replace a tool's output with updatedToolOutput, before Claude ever sees it.
There's also additionalContext, which appends rather than replaces.
So: a PostToolUse hook returning updatedToolOutput with just the matching lines, plus a path to the saved raw output.
Keeping that path back to the raw output is what makes trimming reversible.
Without it, trimming is destruction.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: an async PostToolUse hook that trims in the background, so the agent is never slowed.
Why?
An async hook can't modify anything.
And by the time it finishes, the agent has already swallowed all forty thousand tokens.
Wrong: a PreCompact hook that archives the transcript.
Why?
That preserves a record before summarisation.
But it does nothing to stop the window filling up.
Wrong: a system prompt telling the assistant to ignore irrelevant lines.
Why?
The tokens are spent the moment the result lands in context.
Whether the model ignores them or not.
Hold on to this line.
Trim big results on the way in.
And always keep a path back to the full version.
That trap about async deserves its own moment.
The exam uses it in several disguises.
In plain words, some hooks can say "carry on, I'll finish this in the background."
That's fine for writing a log.
But it's useless for anything that's supposed to change what happens.
Why?
Because by the time the hook finishes, the moment has passed.
The technical name is an async hook output. async set to true in TypeScript.
Or async_ set to True in Python.
With an optional asyncTimeout.
The agent proceeds without waiting.
An async hook cannot block, modify, or inject context.
So async is right for logging, metrics and webhooks.
And wrong for normalisation, denials, and output replacement.
The notes have two questions on this.
Question four.
Here's the scenario.
An engineer writes a PreToolUse hook to redirect writes into a sandbox folder.
It sends the new path to an audit service.
It sets updatedInput.
And it returns async true.
The audit service receives every path.
But files still land in the original locations.
Why?
Take a second.
The answer.
The async return.
The rewrite is discarded, because the agent already moved on.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: updatedInput needs a deny decision.
Why?
That inverts the pairing.
Wrong: the timeout was too long.
Why?
That invents a mechanism.
Question five.
Here's the scenario.
A migration agent must block disallowed database statements, with a reason.
And also audit every attempt, without ever slowing down.
What's the design?
Take a second.
The answer.
Split the jobs.
A synchronous PreToolUse hook that denies with a permissionDecisionReason.
Plus a separate async hook for the audit write.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: a single async PreToolUse hook.
Why?
It can't deny.
Wrong: a PostToolUse hook.
Why?
It fires after the statement already ran.
Wrong: a PermissionRequest hook plus a Stop hook.
Why?
That never blocks anything.
Hold on to this line.
If a hook is meant to change the outcome, it must be synchronous.
Async is for logging only.
Now, what happens when two hooks disagree?
Question six.
Here's the scenario.
A CI agent, meaning continuous integration, has two PreToolUse hooks matched to Bash.
A normalisation hook rewrites commands to use absolute paths, and returns allow with updatedInput.
A security hook returns deny for any command touching production credentials.
An engineer worries that if the normalisation hook runs last, its allow will override the security hook's deny.
What change is needed?
Take a second.
Two managers review a purchase.
One approves.
One vetoes.
Company policy says any veto stops the purchase, whoever signed first.
Nobody needs to reorder the signatures for the veto to count.
The answer.
In exam terms, when several hooks or rules apply to one call, the precedence is deny, then defer, then ask, then allow.
The deny wins, regardless of registration order.
So no change is needed.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: register the security hook after the normalisation hook.
Why?
Order doesn't decide the outcome.
Precedence does.
Wrong: merge both hooks into one callback.
Why?
That couples two concerns with different owners, for nothing.
Wrong: make the normalisation hook async, so it can't interfere.
Why?
An async hook can't modify input.
So path normalisation would quietly stop working.
A quick cross-domain note.
The configuration chapter lists several things that resolve in different directions.
CLAUDE.md scopes are additive.
Skill name collisions go enterprise, then personal, then project.
And hook decisions go deny, defer, ask, allow.
The exam likes to set those against each other.
Now the contrast for this part.
PreToolUse versus PostToolUse.
PreToolUse acts on what's going in, before the tool runs.
Use it to prevent an action.
To enforce a prerequisite.
Or to fix malformed arguments.
PostToolUse acts on what's coming back, after the tool has run, but before the model sees it.
Use it to normalise, trim, annotate, or audit.
The classic wrong answer uses PostToolUse to prevent an action.
It can't.
By the time it fires, the action has happened.
That's part five.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Hooks run in your code.
They cost nothing in context.
And they can't be argued with.
PreToolUse guards the way out.
PostToolUse cleans the way back.
Deny always wins.
And anything that must change the outcome is never async.
Coming up in part six: decomposing complex work.
